title: Britons back ban on trade with Israeli settlements by more than two to one – European Council on Foreign Relations
gist: Opinium polling for ECFR finds UK adults back a ban on trade with Israeli settlements by 46% to 18% (72-28 excluding don't-knows), with support exceeding opposition in every political, regional, age and gender group — giving the British government room to extend restrictions beyond goods into investment, financial services and settlement real estate.

insights.claim: Just 18% of UK adults oppose a ban on trade in goods with Israeli settlements in the West Bank and East Jerusalem against 46% who back it — roughly 72% to 28% once those without an opinion are excluded.
insights.so_what: Quantifies the domestic political cost of settlement-linked commerce in the UK as near zero, which lowers the bar for further restrictive measures.
insights.locator: With the British government set to announce new measures
insights.speaker: Hugh Lovatt

insights.claim: Support crosses every cleavage in British politics: Conservative and Reform voters are more likely to support than oppose the ban, supporters outnumber opponents among both Remain and Leave voters, and support exceeds opposition in every English region, Wales, Scotland, London and Northern Ireland.
insights.so_what: Removes the assumption that settlement measures are a left-coded policy with electoral downside — there is no constituency to lose.
insights.locator: The findings cross the Brexit divide too
insights.speaker: Hugh Lovatt

insights.claim: Only 16% of British adults consider it antisemitic to target Israeli settlements, undercutting the main rhetorical defence against settlement-specific measures.
insights.so_what: The framing risk that has historically deterred governments and companies from settlement divestment does not hold with the UK public.
insights.locator: The polling also finds that only 16% of British adults
insights.speaker: Hugh Lovatt

insights.claim: A two-state solution remains by far the most popular outcome among Britons at 40%, against 12% for a single shared state and just 8% who prefer the status quo of Israel without a Palestinian state.
insights.so_what: Anchors the durable direction of UK policy regardless of which party governs.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, a two-state solution remains by far
insights.speaker: Hugh Lovatt

insights.claim: The UK has so far sanctioned some two dozen organisations and individuals linked to settler violence and excluded settlement goods from preferential tariffs on Israeli products, but stopped short of an outright trade ban that was expected to be announced the day this piece was published.
insights.so_what: Marks the exact policy step-change: from tariff differentiation to prohibition, which is the point at which corporate compliance obligations shift.
insights.locator: To date, the UK has sanctioned some two dozen organisations
insights.speaker: Hugh Lovatt

insights.claim: Public support exists for going much further than goods: extending the ban to investment and financial services, excluding settlements from all UK agreements with Israel including the double-taxation convention, and prohibiting British purchase of settlement real estate.
insights.so_what: The second-order exposure sits in financial services, tax treaties and property — far broader than the goods-trade headline suggests.
insights.locator: The results also suggest the UK government has the public support
insights.speaker: Hugh Lovatt

insights.claim: Named candidates for further sanctions are the organisations instrumental in funding and sustaining the settlement project: Ateret Cohanim, the Jewish National Fund's Himnuta real-estate subsidiary and the Settlement Division of the World Zionist Organization.
insights.so_what: Specific entity names to screen for in counterparty and real-estate due diligence if UK measures widen.
insights.locator: This should go hand-in-hand with additional sanctions
insights.speaker: Hugh Lovatt

insights.claim: Settlement expansion is a state-driven project sustained by domestic economic incentives and foreign financial linkages, so a trade ban attacks the underlying drivers rather than only the most violent manifestation targeted by individual sanctions.
insights.so_what: The analytical case for why economic instruments, not individual designations, are the ones that would actually bite.
insights.quote: However settlement expansion is a state-driven project sustained by domestic economic incentives and foreign financial linkages.
insights.locator: To date, the UK has sanctioned some two dozen
insights.speaker: Hugh Lovatt

insights.claim: UK action would build on similar moves by Belgium, Ireland, the Netherlands and Spain in recent months, indicating a broader European wave of settlement-specific economic restrictions.
insights.so_what: Cross-border regulatory convergence risk for any firm with settlement-linked supply or investment exposure in Europe.
insights.locator: This would build on similar moves by Belgium
insights.speaker: Hugh Lovatt

insights.claim: The policy anchor is the ICJ's 2024 advisory opinion on Israel's occupation, which underscored states' duty to prevent trade or investment relations that assist in maintaining the illegal situation, alongside UN Security Council Resolution 2334 from 2016.
insights.so_what: The legal hook that makes these measures defensible and replicable across jurisdictions — expect it cited in future national legislation.
insights.quote: take steps to prevent trade or investment relations that assist in the maintenance of the illegal situation created by Israel in the Occupied Palestinian Territory
insights.locator: At the heart of the new UK government’s policy reset
insights.speaker: Hugh Lovatt

insights.claim: The British foreign secretary has pledged to go further in challenging Israeli actions destroying the possibility of a two-state solution, citing the recent construction of the “doomsday” E-1 settlement on the outskirts of East Jerusalem.
insights.so_what: E-1 is the named trigger event driving the current escalation in British policy.
